title: Enums
summary: An enum gives a set of named choices a shared name.

subtopics.title: Named choices
subtopics.explanation: An enum gives a name to each allowed option, such as `Pending` or `Shipped`. It is like a menu listing the choices a customer may select. Enums can make code readable, but understand what JavaScript output your TypeScript configuration emits. For example, an order status can move from Pending to Shipped, but an unknown label should be rejected at the data boundary. For example, a status union can reject a misspelled state during type checking.

subtopics.title: Numeric enums
subtopics.explanation: Numeric enums assign numbers to choices, often starting at zero. These values can be difficult to understand in logs or saved data. It is like seeing “status 2” without its label. Use explicit values or another representation when values must remain stable across systems. For example, numeric enum values can appear as numbers in logs, which makes an incident harder to understand. For example, log string states when support needs to understand a failed order.

subtopics.title: String enums
subtopics.explanation: String enums assign readable text values to choices. They can make logs and serialized data clearer. It is like printing the full label on a ticket. Check how values are stored and compared, especially when an API expects a specific spelling. For example, a string value such as "shipped" is easier to inspect in an API payload than an unexplained number. For example, choose stable wire values before saving them in a database.

subtopics.title: Union alternative
subtopics.explanation: A union such as `type Status = "pending" | "shipped"` can limit a value without creating an enum object at runtime. It is like a menu whose options are written directly on the form. Literal unions work well for many simple state values. For example, a literal union is often enough for a small fixed set of UI states. For example, check unknown server values instead of assuming every enum option arrived.

subtopics.title: Use consistently
subtopics.explanation: Choose one representation and use it consistently across code, APIs, and saved data. Changing a value later can break stored records or clients. It is like agreeing on the exact label before printing thousands of tickets. Validate values received from outside TypeScript. For example, changing a serialized value can break old records, so coordinate the representation with the API. For example, use exhaustive switching so adding a new state reveals incomplete handling.

foundations.overview: An enum gives names to a fixed set of related choices, such as order states. TypeScript also supports unions of literal values, which can be simpler in many applications. Think of them as labels on a small set of allowed buttons. Choose a representation that works well in code and when values cross a network or storage boundary.
foundations.whyItMatters: Enums and literal unions encode finite choices. Their runtime output and serialized values matter when the choices cross module, API, or storage boundaries.
foundations.mentalModel: An enum gives names to a fixed set of related choices, such as order states.
foundations.browserPerspective: TypeScript checks enum usage before producing JavaScript.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use named statuses when code branches on a small set of meaningful states.
foundations.businessImpact: Clear states help teams discuss how work moves through a product.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Choose one representation consistently across API boundaries.
foundations.performanceImpact: Use the simplest representation that fits the application.
commonUseCases: Represent a checkout state consistently in the UI and API.
Read status values in logs during support investigations.
Reject an unrecognized state sent by a server.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An enum is only a compile-time label.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Depending on configuration, TypeScript enums can create runtime JavaScript output.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Numeric enum values are self-explanatory in stored data.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A value such as 2 is unclear without its mapping and can be fragile across systems.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A union and enum always behave identically.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unions are erased types; enums may create runtime values, so choose based on actual needs.

visualExplorer.title: How a numeric enum compiles and reverse-maps
visualExplorer.caption: Step through declaring a numeric enum and see the two-way map TypeScript builds.

config.intro: Trace enum Direction { Up, Down } from declaration to its emitted runtime object.

steps.name: Declare members
steps.detail: enum Direction { Up, Down } lists named members with no explicit values.

steps.name: Auto-increment
steps.detail: TypeScript assigns Up = 0 and Down = 1, incrementing from zero.

steps.name: Emit an object
steps.detail: It compiles to a JavaScript object: { Up: 0, Down: 1 } built inside an IIFE.

steps.name: Add reverse keys
steps.detail: For numeric enums it also writes { 0: 'Up', 1: 'Down' }, creating a two-way map.

steps.name: Use either direction
steps.detail: Now Direction.Up is 0 and Direction[0] is 'Up' — name-to-value and value-to-name both work.

interactiveExamples.title: Numeric enum and reverse mapping
interactiveExamples.explanation: Numeric members auto-increment from 0, and you can map a value back to its name.

sandbox.code:
enum Direction {
  Up,
  Down,
  Left,
  Right
}

console.log(Direction.Up);    // 0
console.log(Direction.Right); // 3
console.log(Direction[0]);    // 'Up' (reverse mapping)

interactiveExamples.title: String enum (no reverse mapping)
interactiveExamples.explanation: String enums hold readable values, but reverse lookup returns undefined.

sandbox.code:
enum Status {
  Active = 'ACTIVE',
  Done = 'DONE'
}

console.log(Status.Active);        // 'ACTIVE'
console.log(Status['ACTIVE']);     // undefined (no reverse map)
console.log(Object.keys(Status));  // ['Active', 'Done']
